newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban ultimatum to Rabbani military chief.
newsitem.headline: Taleban ultimatum to Rabbani military chief.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban militia on Tuesday issued a surrender-or-else ultimatum to the military chief of the government it ousted from Kabul and squared off against a powerful northern warlord.

As international concern mounted over the situation in the war-ravaged country, the commander of Taleban forces which swept north after capturing the capital Kabul last Friday said he had called on Ahmad Shah Masood to give up or be wiped out.
Masood, military chief in ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government, withdrew to his Panjsher heartland base when Kabul fell to the Taleban with hardly a shot being fired.
Taleban commander Abdur Razzaq told Reuters in Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of Panjsher valley he sent Masood a letter saying that if he stopped fighting "we will forgive him".
But, he added: "If he goes on fighting, we will clear the area of his presence."

After capturing Jabal os-Siraj, a Masood stronghold 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul, the Taleban pushed towards Salang Tunnel -- and came into direct confrontation with the organised army of warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum for the first time.
Dostum had previously stayed clear of the fighting between the Taleban militia and forces of the Rabbani government.
Officials with Dostum's well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction said they would fight if the Taleban pushed further north.
Razzaq set no deadline for Masood to respond to his ultimatum, but Taleban fighters reported orders to move early on Wednesday against the Panjsher and the Uzbek forces of Dostum.
"The orders have been given. We move against the Panjsher and Dostum early tomorrow," said one Taleban fighter.
Razzaq said however he did not want to fight Dostum, whose headquarters are in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Military experts said on Tuesday that Masood and Dostum may have to bury an old rivalry to confront the Taleban.
While the two-year-old Taleban militia's sweeping gains give it control of three-quarters of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, foreign military experts would not write off Dostum and Masood.
"Much will depend on whether he (Masood) and Dostum can put their enmity aside and cooperate against the Taleban," one military source said.
Dostum, once defence minister in Rabbani's government, was involved in an attempt to seize Kabul in a military coup on January 1, 1994, setting off bloody fighting with Masood forces.

The chorus of world concern was led by Russia. It proposed leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) meet to work out steps to prevent the upsurge of fighting in Afghanistan from spilling into former Soviet territory.
Yeltsin, in hospital awaiting heart surgery, told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to contact some leaders of the 12-member commonwealth, his press office said in a statement.
Russia's national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying the Taleban triumph was fraught with danger for Moscow and CIS partners in central Asia.

"If Taleban, backed by Pakistan, reaches the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, parts of which including the city of Bukhara they want to annexe, they will wipe away Russian border posts and see the road to the north free," he said.
Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan in 1979 but withdrew some 10 years later after failing to put down guerrilla resistance.
United Nations' special envoy Norbert Holl said he was trying to arrange peace talks among Afghan warring factions.
He told German radio he would visit two more groups after his meeting with the dominant Taleban Islamic militia.
In New Delhi, about 400 Afghan refugees protested against the Taleban and said they were praying for the militia's ouster.
Nearly 25,000 Afghans fled to India after Soviet-backed General Najibullah was ousted from power in 1992. The Taleban executed Najibullah after overrunning Kabul last week.
The Rabbani government meanwhile refused to give up office and urged the U.N. to probe Pakistani support for the Taleban.
Pakistan, which denies accusations it backs the Taleban, sent a diplomat to Kabul this week to reopen its embassy there.
The United States toughened its line towards the Taleban by condemning the execution of Najibullah and stressing concerns over such issues as terrorism and narcotics.
The United States has not had an embassy in Kabul since 1989 due to civil war and there has not been a U.S. ambassador in the country since 1979, when its envoy was assassinated.

Decisions on many issues, including whether women will be allowed to work and girls will be allowed to go to school, have been referred to the Taleban's Kandahar-based supreme council led by Mullah Mohammad Omar, who founded the movement in 1994.

In Nasir Bagh, Pakistan, relief workers and authorities were trying to persuade thousands of Afghan refugees to return home after the Taleban took the capital Kabul, but many women refugees said they were suspicious and afraid of the new rulers.
Women who fled the horrors of 17 years of war said life would be impossible under strict Taleban fundamentalist limits.
